cse-2001-b-61-a.approach: Let $f(s)$ be the string printed by `abc(s)`. Each call prints the output of the suffix call twice and then its own first character, so build the output from the shortest suffix upward.

steps.title: Write the recurrence
steps.body:
`abc(s)` does: `abc(s+1)`, `abc(s+1)`, then prints `s[0]`. So

$$f(s) = f(s+1)\,f(s+1)\,s[0], \qquad f(\text{empty string}) = \varepsilon$$

scene.caption: abc("3"): two empty calls, then print 3

answer.value: The program prints **3323321**.

pitfalls: Printing happens after both recursive calls, so the first character `1` appears only once, at the very end.
Do not reverse the string: each suffix output is duplicated, not just the characters.
cse-2001-b-61-a.verification: Length check: $2^3 - 1 = 7$ characters, matching part (b); the counts are one 1, two 2s and four 3s, as in 3323321.

cse-2001-b-61-b.approach: Count characters with a recurrence: a call on a length-$n$ string makes two calls on length $n-1$ and prints one character.

steps.title: Set up the recurrence
steps.body:
Let $T(n)$ be the number of characters printed for a string of length $n$. The empty string prints nothing and every other call prints one character after two calls on the suffix:

$$T(0) = 0, \qquad T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1$$

steps.title: Check with n = 3
steps.body: $T(1) = 1$, $T(2) = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 = 3$, $T(3) = 2 \cdot 3 + 1 = 7 = 2^3 - 1$, matching the 7 characters of 3323321.

answer.value: $2^n - 1$ characters

cse-2001-b-61-b.shortcut: The character at index $i$ (0-based) is printed $2^i$ times, so the total is $1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1$.
pitfalls: The base case is the empty string, which prints nothing; using $T(1) = 1$ as the base gives the same result, but $T(0) = 1$ does not.
cse-2001-b-61-b.verification: Summed per-character counts $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} 2^i = 2^n - 1$ and checked $n = 3$ against part (a).

cse-2001-b-62-a.approach: Insert each key by walking down from the root (smaller goes left, larger goes right) and attaching it at the first empty slot.

steps.title: Insert 15, 32, 20
steps.body: 15 becomes the root. $32 > 15$ → right child of 15. $20 > 15$, $20 < 32$ → left child of 32.

steps.title: Insert 9 and 3
steps.body: $9 < 15$ → left child of 15. $3 < 15$, $3 < 9$ → left child of 9.

answer.value: Root 15; left child 9 (children 3 and 12, with 1 as the left child of 3); right child 32 (left child 20, whose right child is 25).

pitfalls: 25 goes to the right of 20, not to the right of 32: compare at every level.
cse-2001-b-62-a.verification: Inorder traversal gives 1, 3, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25, 32 — sorted, so the tree is a valid BST of all eight keys.

cse-2001-b-62-b.approach: 15 has two children, so replace it by its inorder successor (the minimum of its right subtree) and delete the successor from its old place.

steps.title: Classify the node
steps.body: 15 is the root and has two children (9 and 32), so it cannot simply be unlinked.

steps.title: Find the inorder successor
steps.body: Go right once to 32, then left as far as possible: 32 → 20. 20 has no left child, so the successor is **20**.

steps.title: Replace and splice
steps.body: Copy 20 into the root. The old node 20 had only a right child 25, so 25 takes its place as the left child of 32.

answer.value: Root 20; left subtree unchanged (9 with children 3 and 12, 1 below 3); right child 32 with left child 25.

pitfalls: Forgetting to re-attach 25 when 20 is moved up.
Using the inorder predecessor (12) is also a valid textbook method; it gives root 12 with 9 having only the left child 3. State which convention you use.

cse-2001-b-62-c.approach: Depth of a tree = 1 + the larger of the depths of its two subtrees; the code already has the left depth in `x`, so compute the right depth in `y` and return 1 plus the maximum.

steps.title: Recursive definition
steps.body: $\text{depth}(\text{NULL}) = 0$ and $\text{depth}(t) = 1 + \max(\text{depth}(t\to\text{left}),\ \text{depth}(t\to\text{right}))$.

steps.title: Fill in the blanks
Check on a small tree
steps.body: For a single node: $x = 0$, $y = 0$, the `else` branch returns $1 + 0 = 1$. For the root 15 of part (a): left depth 3 (9 → 3 → 1), right depth 3 (32 → 20 → 25), so it returns $1 + 3 = 4$.

answer.value: S1: `y = depth(t->right);` S2: `return 1 + x;` S3: `return 1 + y;`

pitfalls: Returning `x` or `y` without adding 1 makes every tree have depth 0.
cse-2001-b-62-c.verification: Traced a one-node tree and the tree of part (a) (4 levels).

cse-2001-b-63-a.approach: Run Kruskal: take edges in increasing weight and keep each one that joins two different components. With only 8 edges this is quick and also exposes the tie needed for part (b).

steps.title: Weights 2 and 3
steps.body: Take n1–n2 (2) and n1–n6 (3); component $\{n1, n2, n6\}$.

steps.title: The two weight-4 edges
steps.body: n2–n4 joins n4 to $\{n1,n2,n6\}$ — take it. Then n4–n6 would close the cycle n4–n2–n1–n6–n4 — reject. (Taking n4–n6 first and rejecting n2–n4 is equally valid.)

steps.title: Weights 7, 8, 9, 12
steps.body: n3–n4 (7) adds n3 — take. n1–n3 (8): both ends already connected — reject. n4–n5 (9) adds n5 — take. Now 5 edges span all 6 vertices; n2–n5 (12) is rejected.

answer.value: Edges (n1,n2,2), (n1,n6,3), (n2,n4,4), (n3,n4,7), (n4,n5,9) — total weight 25. Replacing (n2,n4,4) by (n4,n6,4) gives the other MST.

pitfalls: The vertex is printed as "p5" in the paper but the edges use n5 — it is a typo.
n4–n5 (9) is needed even though n2–n5 exists: 12 is heavier.

cse-2001-b-63-b.approach: Different MSTs can only arise from ties. Every edge except the two weight-4 edges is forced, and exactly one of those two must be chosen.

steps.title: Forced edges
steps.body: Weights 2, 3, 7, 9 are unique and each is accepted by Kruskal no matter how ties are broken; 8 and 12 always close cycles. So n1–n2, n1–n6, n3–n4, n4–n5 are in every MST.

steps.title: The tie
steps.body: n2–n4 and n4–n6 (both 4) each connect n4 to the component $\{n1, n2, n6\}$. Exactly one can be used — taking both forms the cycle n4–n2–n1–n6–n4.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: $1 \times 2 = 2$ distinct MSTs, each of weight 25.

pitfalls: Equal weights do not automatically double the count: check that the tied edges really are interchangeable (here they are, because they lie on one cycle).
cse-2001-b-63-b.verification: Both trees have weight $2 + 3 + 4 + 7 + 9 = 25$ and no other spanning tree reaches 25 (any other choice brings in 8 or 12).

cse-2001-b-63-c.approach: All MSTs of a graph have the same sorted list of edge weights, so in particular the smallest weight is the same in every MST.

steps.title: Key fact
steps.body: Kruskal with a different tie-break order produces every MST, and for every weight $w$ the number of edges of weight $\le w$ it accepts equals $|V|$ minus the number of components of the subgraph of edges with weight $\le w$ — independent of tie-breaking. Hence all MSTs have the same multiset of weights.

steps.title: Apply to the minimum
steps.body: Moreover a lightest edge of the graph lies in some MST, and no MST can avoid all of them (adding one to an MST and removing a heavier cycle edge would give a lighter tree). So the minimum MST edge weight is always the global minimum weight — the same value for every MST.

steps.title: This graph
steps.body: Both MSTs have weights $\{2, 3, 4, 7, 9\}$; the minimum is 2 in each.

answer.value: **Yes** — the minimum edge weight is the same in every MST (it equals the smallest edge weight of the graph).

pitfalls: "Unique" here refers to the weight value, not to the edge; the lightest edge itself may differ between MSTs when weights tie.
cse-2001-b-63-c.verification: Checked on both MSTs of this graph (minimum 2 in each).

cse-2001-b-63-d.approach: Again use that all MSTs share the same multiset of edge weights; therefore the largest weight in an MST (the bottleneck) is the same for all MSTs.

steps.title: Same multiset
steps.body: For each threshold $w$, every MST contains exactly $|V| - c(w)$ edges of weight $\le w$, where $c(w)$ is the number of components using only edges of weight $\le w$. So the sorted weight lists of all MSTs coincide.

steps.title: Maximum
steps.body: The maximum of identical multisets is identical. Equivalently, it is the smallest $w$ for which the edges of weight $\le w$ connect the graph (the minimum bottleneck value).

steps.title: This graph
steps.body: Edges of weight $\le 7$ leave n5 isolated; adding weight 9 connects it. Both MSTs have maximum weight 9.

answer.value: **Yes** — every MST has the same maximum edge weight.

pitfalls: The heaviest edge itself need not be unique; only its weight is.
cse-2001-b-63-d.verification: Both MSTs of this graph contain (n4,n5,9) as their heaviest edge.

cse-2001-b-64-a.approach: FIRST comes from the leading symbols of each right-hand side; FOLLOW of A inherits FOLLOW(E) (A ends E → aA) and FOLLOW of E inherits FOLLOW(A) (E ends A → +E, A → *E), plus `)` from E → (E) and \$ because E is the start symbol.

steps.title: FIRST sets
steps.body:
E → aA starts with $a$; E → (E) starts with `(`. So $\text{FIRST}(E) = \{a, (\}$.

A → +E, A → *E, A → ε give $\text{FIRST}(A) = \{+, *, \varepsilon\}$.

steps.title: FOLLOW constraints
steps.body:
- E is the start symbol: $\$ \in \text{FOLLOW}(E)$.
- E → ( E ): $) \in \text{FOLLOW}(E)$.
- E → a A (A at the end): $\text{FOLLOW}(E) \subseteq \text{FOLLOW}(A)$.
- A → + E and A → * E (E at the end): $\text{FOLLOW}(A) \subseteq \text{FOLLOW}(E)$.

steps.title: Solve
steps.body:
The two inclusions make the sets equal, and the only terminals contributed are `)` and \$:

$$\text{FOLLOW}(E) = \text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{\,),\ \$\,\}$$

answer.value: FIRST(E) = {a, (}; FIRST(A) = {+, *, ε}; FOLLOW(E) = FOLLOW(A) = {), \$}.

pitfalls: The paper says "start symbol B", a misprint for E; without it E would not get \$.
+ and * are not in FOLLOW(E) — they never appear after E in any production.
cse-2001-b-64-a.verification: Derivation $E \Rightarrow (E) \Rightarrow (aA) \Rightarrow (a)$ shows `)` after A; $E \Rightarrow aA \Rightarrow a$ shows the end marker \$ after A.

cse-2001-b-64-b.approach: Fill M[X, t] with X → α for each t in FIRST(α); when α can derive ε, also for each t in FOLLOW(X). Use the FIRST/FOLLOW sets of part (a).

steps.title: Rows for E
steps.body: FIRST(aA) = {a} → M[E, a] = E → aA. FIRST((E)) = {(} → M[E, (] = E → (E).

steps.title: Rows for A
steps.body: M[A, +] = A → +E, M[A, *] = A → *E. A → ε goes under FOLLOW(A) = {), \$}: M[A, )] = M[A, \$] = A → ε.

steps.title: Check for conflicts
steps.body: Every cell holds at most one production, so the grammar is LL(1). Blank cells are error entries.

answer.value: M[E,a] = E→aA; M[E,(] = E→(E); M[A,+] = A→+E; M[A,*] = A→*E; M[A,)] = M[A,\$] = A→ε; all other entries are errors. No cell has two entries, so the grammar is LL(1).

pitfalls: Placing A → ε under FIRST instead of FOLLOW.
cse-2001-b-64-b.verification: Parsed `(a+a)`: E→(E), E→aA, A→+E, E→aA, A→ε on `)`, then match `)` and accept on \$.

cse-2001-b-65.approach: A repeat-until loop runs its body first and tests afterwards, so one label at the top of the body is enough: emit label, body code, condition code, then jump back to the label while the condition variable is 0 (false).

steps.title: Code layout
steps.body:
```
L:  S1.code
    E.code              // leaves 1/0 in E.varName
    if E.varName = 0 goto L
```
Falling through the conditional jump (E true) exits the loop.

steps.title: Semantic rules
steps.body:
For $S \to \text{repeat } S_1 \text{ until } E$:

```
S.begin = newlabel();
S.code  = gen(S.begin ":")
          || S1.code
          || E.code
          || gen("if " E.varName " = 0 goto " S.begin);
```

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body: The body executes once before any test. After each iteration $E$ is evaluated; value 0 jumps back to `S.begin`, value 1 falls through to the next statement, which is exactly "repeat until $E$ is true".

answer.value: S.begin = newlabel(); S.code = gen(S.begin ":") || S1.code || E.code || gen("if" E.varName "= 0 goto" S.begin)

pitfalls: Testing the condition before the body (that is a while loop).
Jumping back when E is true — repeat-until loops while E is false.
cse-2001-b-65.verification: Traced `repeat x = x + 1 until x > 2` from x = 0: the body runs for x = 0, 1, 2, test values 0, 0, 1, exit after the third pass.

cse-2001-b-66-a.approach: Apply the standard rule: $A \to A\alpha_1 \mid A\alpha_2 \mid \beta_1 \mid \beta_2$ becomes $A \to \beta_1 A' \mid \beta_2 A'$, $A' \to \alpha_1 A' \mid \alpha_2 A' \mid \varepsilon$.

steps.title: Identify α and β
steps.body: In $S \to Sa \mid Sb \mid a \mid b$: the left-recursive tails are $\alpha_1 = a$, $\alpha_2 = b$; the non-recursive alternatives are $\beta_1 = a$, $\beta_2 = b$.

steps.title: Rewrite
steps.body:
$$S \to aS' \mid bS'$$
$$S' \to aS' \mid bS' \mid \varepsilon$$

steps.title: Language check
steps.body: Both grammars generate $(a+b)(a+b)^*$: a first symbol from $\{a, b\}$ followed by any string over $\{a, b\}$.

answer.value: S → aS' | bS';  S' → aS' | bS' | ε

pitfalls: Forgetting S' → ε, which would make the grammar generate no finite strings.
cse-2001-b-66-a.verification: Derived `aba` in both: $S \Rightarrow Sa \Rightarrow Sba \Rightarrow aba$ and $S \Rightarrow aS' \Rightarrow abS' \Rightarrow abaS' \Rightarrow aba$.

cse-2001-b-66-b.approach: abab starts with a, so the root must use S → aSbS. Split abab = a·X·b·Y where X and Y are strings of the grammar (equal numbers of a and b) and count the splits.

steps.title: Root production
steps.body: Only S → aSbS can start with `a`, so abab = a X b Y with X b Y = bab, where X and Y must each have as many a’s as b’s.

steps.title: Possible splits
steps.body:
| X | Y | valid? |
|---|---|---|
| ε | ab | yes |
| ba | ε | yes |
| bab | — | no (no b left) |

X = ε, Y = ab: Y uses S → aSbS with both inner S → ε. X = ba, Y = ε: X uses S → bSaS with both inner S → ε.

steps.title: Tree 1
steps.body: S → a S b S, first S → ε, second S → a S b S (both ε): $a\,(\varepsilon)\,b\,(ab)$.

steps.title: Tree 2
steps.body: S → a S b S, first S → b S a S (both ε), second S → ε: $a\,(ba)\,b\,(\varepsilon)$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: abab has exactly two distinct parse trees (two leftmost derivations), so the grammar is **ambiguous**.

answer.value: Two parse trees: S → aSbS with (S → ε, S → aSbS → ab) and S → aSbS with (S → bSaS → ba, S → ε). The grammar is **ambiguous**.

pitfalls: One parse tree per split: inner S → ε is forced in every sub-derivation, so there are no more than two trees.
cse-2001-b-66-b.verification: Leftmost derivations: $S \Rightarrow aSbS \Rightarrow abS \Rightarrow abaSbS \Rightarrow ababS \Rightarrow abab$ and $S \Rightarrow aSbS \Rightarrow abSaSbS \Rightarrow abaSbS \Rightarrow ababS \Rightarrow abab$ differ at step 2.

cse-2001-b-67-a.approach: A violation needs P1 to pass its R2 test while P2 has not yet marked R2 busy, and P2 to pass its R1 test while P1 has not yet marked R1 busy. Write these as ordering constraints and show they form a cycle.

steps.title: What a violation needs
steps.body:
Both in the critical section (S5 and Q5) at once means P1 passed S3 and P2 passed Q3 without either having released anything.

- P1 passes S3 only if R2 is free then: $S3 < Q2$.
- P2 passes Q3 only if R1 is free then: $Q3 < S2$.

steps.title: Program order
steps.body: Inside each process: $S2 < S3$ and $Q2 < Q3$.

steps.title: Contradiction
steps.body: Chaining: $S2 < S3 < Q2 < Q3 < S2$ — a cycle, impossible. Hence both processes can never be past their second test at the same time.

answer.value: **Yes**, mutual exclusion is guaranteed: a violation would require $S2 < S3 < Q2 < Q3 < S2$, which is impossible.

pitfalls: Test-and-set is not atomic here, which tempts one to claim a violation; but each process sets its first resource busy before testing the second, and the two tests cannot both succeed.
cse-2001-b-67-a.verification: Tried the natural attack S1, Q1, S2, Q2: then S3 sees R2 busy and Q3 sees R1 busy — they block (deadlock, part b) rather than both entering.

cse-2001-b-67-b.approach: P1 grabs R1 then R2 and P2 grabs R2 then R1 — opposite orders, the classic circular wait. Let each take its first resource and both spin forever.

steps.title: Interleaving
steps.body:
| Step | Statement | R1 | R2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | S1 (R1 free) | free | free |
| 2 | S2 | busy (P1) | free |
| 3 | Q1 (R2 free) | busy | free |
| 4 | Q2 | busy | busy (P2) |
| 5 | S3: R2 busy, spin | busy | busy |
| 6 | Q3: R1 busy, spin | busy | busy |

steps.title: Why it never ends
steps.body: P1 frees R1 only at S6, after it gets R2; P2 frees R2 only at Q6, after it gets R1. Each waits for the other: circular wait, so neither progresses.

answer.value: **Yes**: S1, S2, Q1, Q2 — then P1 spins at S3 waiting for R2 and P2 spins at Q3 waiting for R1 forever.

pitfalls: Busy-waiting processes are not "blocked" in the scheduler sense, but they still make no progress — this is a deadlock.
cse-2001-b-67-b.verification: All four Coffman conditions hold: exclusive use, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1.

cse-2001-b-67-c.approach: After the swap both processes acquire R1 first, then R2. That removes circular wait (no deadlock), but because the busy-test and the set are separate statements, both can pass both tests before either sets.

steps.title: New P2
Mutual exclusion fails
steps.body: Interleaving S1, Q1, S2, Q2, S3, Q3, S4, Q4: both see R1 free (S1, Q1), both set it, both see R2 free (S3, Q3), both set it, and both execute "Use R1 and R2" (S5, Q5) together.

steps.title: No deadlock
steps.body: Both request in the same order R1 → R2, so no circular wait. A process waiting at its R2 test is waiting for the other process, which already holds (or passed) R1 and needs nothing else, so it reaches S6/S7 or Q6/Q7 and frees R2. A process waiting at its R1 test waits for one that will finish the same way.

answer.value: Mutual exclusion is **not** guaranteed (e.g. S1, Q1, S2, Q2, S3, Q3, S4, Q4 lets both use R1 and R2); deadlock **cannot** occur.

pitfalls: Ordered acquisition prevents deadlock but does not by itself make a non-atomic check-then-set safe.
cse-2001-b-67-c.verification: For deadlock both would have to wait forever; one is always ahead in the common order R1 → R2 and can finish.

cse-2001-b-68-a.approach: Elevator (LOOK) from 25 moving up: serve 32 and 45, then reverse and serve 10, 7, 5. Seek time = tracks moved × 0.2 ms.

steps.title: Service order
steps.body:
Requests above 25: 32, 45 (served going up). Below 25: 10, 7, 5 (served on the way down).

Order: 25 → 32 → 45 → 10 → 7 → 5.

steps.title: Seek time
steps.body:
$60 \times 0.2\ \text{ms} = 12\ \text{ms}$.

If the head is assumed to travel to the last track 99 before reversing (SCAN), it is $(99 - 25) + (99 - 5) = 74 + 94 = 168$ tracks $= 33.6$ ms.

answer.value: **12 ms** (60 tracks × 0.2 ms: 25 → 45 → 5). If the elevator must go to track 99 before reversing, 33.6 ms.

pitfalls: Adding rotational latency — the question asks only for seek time.

cse-2001-b-68-b.approach: Bound the three components separately: starting at track 0 the elevator sweeps up at most once (≤ 99 tracks), and each of the 100 requests can suffer at most one full rotation of latency plus one sector transfer.

steps.title: Disk parameters
steps.body: 3000 rpm → $60 / 3000 = 0.02$ s = **20 ms** per rotation. 100 sectors per track → transfer of one sector = $20 / 100 = 0.2$ ms.

steps.title: Seek
steps.body: Head at track 0 and no new arrivals, so the elevator only moves up; the farthest it can go is track 99: $99 \times 0.2 = 19.8$ ms.

steps.title: Latency and transfer
steps.body: Worst case each request just missed its sector: latency ≈ one full rotation, 20 ms; then 0.2 ms to read it. For 100 requests: $100 \times (20 + 0.2) = 2020$ ms.

answer.value: ≈ **2039.8 ms** (19.8 ms seek + 100 × (20 ms rotation + 0.2 ms transfer)).

pitfalls: Taking the average latency (10 ms) instead of the worst case.
Counting a reverse sweep — starting at track 0 there is nothing below the head.
cse-2001-b-68-b.verification: If the worst latency is taken as $20 - 0.2 = 19.8$ ms (the sector cannot be missed by a full rotation exactly) the total becomes $19.8 + 100 \times 20 = 2019.8$ ms — the same order; the stored answer uses the simpler full-rotation bound.

cse-2001-b-69-a.approach: A name appears more than once exactly when two tuples with different regno share it. Take the product of two renamed copies, keep pairs with equal name and different regno, and project the name.

steps.title: Two copies
steps.body: $\rho_{e1}(\text{examinee}) \times \rho_{e2}(\text{examinee})$ pairs every tuple with every tuple.

steps.title: Select duplicates
steps.body: Keep pairs with $e1.\text{name} = e2.\text{name} \land e1.\text{regno} \ne e2.\text{regno}$ — two different examinees (regno is the key) with the same name.

steps.title: Project
steps.body:
$$\Pi_{e1.\text{name}}\big(\sigma_{e1.\text{name} = e2.\text{name} \,\land\, e1.\text{regno} \ne e2.\text{regno}}(\rho_{e1}(\text{examinee}) \times \rho_{e2}(\text{examinee}))\big)$$
Projection removes duplicate names.

answer.value: $\Pi_{e1.name}(\sigma_{e1.name = e2.name \land e1.regno \ne e2.regno}(\rho_{e1}(examinee) \times \rho_{e2}(examinee)))$

pitfalls: Omitting $e1.regno \ne e2.regno$: every tuple matches itself, so every name would be returned.
cse-2001-b-69-a.verification: With tuples (1, Ann), (2, Ann), (3, Bob): only the pairs (1,2) and (2,1) survive, giving {Ann}.

cse-2001-b-69-b.approach: Compare each score with a scalar subquery that computes the overall average.

steps.title: Average
steps.body: `SELECT AVG(score) FROM examinee` returns a single value.

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT regno
FROM examinee
WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM examinee);
```

answer.value: `SELECT regno FROM examinee WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM examinee);`

pitfalls: `WHERE score > AVG(score)` is illegal: aggregates cannot appear in WHERE without a subquery.
cse-2001-b-69-b.verification: Scores 50, 70, 90 → average 70 → only the examinee with 90 is listed.

cse-2001-b-69-c.approach: Join appears with examinee on regno, filter score > 80, and project the centre code with DISTINCT.

steps.title: Join and filter
steps.body: Match each appearance with its examinee (`a.regno = e.regno`) and keep rows with `e.score > 80`.

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT a.centr_code
FROM appears a, examinee e
WHERE a.regno = e.regno AND e.score > 80;
```
DISTINCT lists each centre once even if several of its examinees qualify.

answer.value: `SELECT DISTINCT a.centr_code FROM appears a, examinee e WHERE a.regno = e.regno AND e.score > 80;`

pitfalls: Without DISTINCT a centre with several high scorers is repeated.
cse-2001-b-69-c.verification: Equivalent form: `SELECT DISTINCT centr_code FROM appears WHERE regno IN (SELECT regno FROM examinee WHERE score > 80);`

cse-2001-b-70-a.approach: Fan-out 3 means at most 2 keys per node. On a leaf overflow keep 2 keys on the left, move 1 to a new right leaf and copy its first key up; on an internal overflow push the middle key up.

steps.title: Insert 80, 50, 10
steps.body: Leaf [50, 80]; inserting 10 gives [10, 50, 80] — overflow. Split into [10, 50] and [80], copy 80 up: root [80].

steps.title: Insert 30
steps.body: Leaf [10, 30, 50] overflows → [10, 30] and [50]; 50 goes up → root [50, 70, 80] overflows. Split the internal node: middle key 70 moves up to a new root; left node [50], right node [80].

steps.title: Insert 90
steps.body: Leaf [80, 90, 100] overflows → [80, 90] and [100]; 100 goes up to the internal node, which becomes [80, 100].

pitfalls: In a B+ tree a leaf split copies the separator up (it stays in the leaf); an internal split moves it up.
Splitting [10, 50, 80] as [10] [50, 80] is the other convention — it gives different (equally valid) trees, so state your choice.
cse-2001-b-70-a.verification: All leaves are at the same depth, every node has at most 2 keys, and a left-to-right leaf scan gives 10, 30, 50, 70, 80, 90, 100.

cse-2001-b-70-b.approach: Minimum occupancy for fan-out 3: a leaf needs at least 1 key, an internal node at least 2 children. Deleting 30 is harmless; deleting 10 empties a leaf, forcing a merge whose parent then underflows and borrows through the root.

steps.title: Delete 30
steps.body: Leaf [10, 30] → [10], still 1 key, so nothing else changes.

steps.title: Delete 10: leaf underflow
steps.body: Leaf [10] becomes empty. Its sibling [50] has only 1 key (cannot lend), so merge: the leaves become [50] and separator 50 is removed from the parent, leaving the left internal node with a single child — underflow.

steps.title: Borrow through the root
steps.body: The right internal node [80, 100] has 3 children, so it lends one: root key 70 comes down into the left node, the leaf [70] moves to the left node, and 80 goes up to the root. Left node [70] → [50] [70]; right node [100] → [80, 90] [100].

pitfalls: Merging the two internal nodes is impossible here (it would need 4 children); redistribution is required.
Separator keys may remain in internal nodes after their leaf entry is deleted; only structure changes need fixing.
cse-2001-b-70-b.verification: Leaf scan: 50, 70, 80, 90, 100; every leaf has ≥ 1 key, every internal node has 2–3 children, all leaves at depth 2.
